Legislative, regulatory, and societal responses to global climate change create financial risk.
We are the world’s leading supplier of hydrogen, the primary use of which is the production of ultra-low sulfur transportation fuels that have significantly reduced transportation emissions and helped improve human health. To make the high volumes of hydrogen needed by our customers, we use steam methane reforming, which produces carbon dioxide. In addition, gasification enables the conversion of lower value feedstocks into cleaner energy and value-added products; however, our gasification projects also produce carbon dioxide. Some of our operations are within jurisdictions that have or are developing regulatory regimes governing GHG emissions, including CO2, which may lead to direct and indirect costs on our operations. Furthermore, some jurisdictions have various mechanisms to target the power sector to achieve emission reductions, which often result in higher power costs. Increased public concern and governmental action may result in more international, U.S. federal and/or regional requirements to reduce or mitigate the effects of GHG emissions. Although uncertain, these developments could increase our costs related to consumption of electric power, hydrogen production and application of our gasification technology. We believe we will be able to mitigate some of the increased costs through contractual terms, but the lack of definitive legislation or regulatory requirements prevents an accurate estimate of the long-term impact these measures will have on our operations. Any legislation or governmental action that limits or taxes GHG emissions could negatively impact our growth, increase our operating costs, or reduce demand for certain of our products.

It explains that regulatory regimes governing GHGs such as CO2 could impose direct and indirect costs, and that mechanisms to reduce emissions in the power sector could increase power costs. It further notes that any legislation or action that limits or taxes GHG emissions could negatively affect growth, operating costs, or demand for products. Other ESG categories like Human Capital or Product Liability are not the main theme; the driver is climate regulation and emissions-related cost and demand risk.

Operational Risks
Our factories, facilities and distribution system are subject to catastrophic loss due to fire, flood, terrorism, public health crises, increasing severity or frequency of extreme weather events, or other climate-change related risks. For example, in the first quarter of fiscal year 2020, the outbreak of COVID-19 in China led to an extension of the Lunar New Year holiday, which adversely impacted our business and results, reduced the number of selling days and otherwise impacted our supply chain. In addition, several of our facilities could be subject to a catastrophic loss caused by earthquake due to their locations. Our production facilities, headquarters and laboratories in California, and our production facilities in Japan, are all located in areas with above-average seismic activity. If any of our facilities were to experience a catastrophic loss, it could disrupt our operations, delay production, shipments and revenue and result in large expenses to repair or replace the facility. If such a disruption were to occur, we could breach agreements, our reputation could be harmed, and our business and operating results could be adversely affected. In addition, because we have consolidated our manufacturing facilities and we may not have redundant manufacturing capability readily available, we are more likely to experience an interruption to our operations in the event of a catastrophe in any one location. Although we carry insurance for property damage and business interruption, we do not carry insurance or financial reserves for interruptions or potential losses arising from earthquakes or terrorism. Also, our third-party insurance coverage will vary from time to time in both type and amount depending on availability, cost and our decisions with respect to risk retention. Economic conditions and uncertainties in global markets may adversely affect the cost and other terms upon which we are able to obtain third-party insurance.

Numerous states, including Washington, Oregon and New York, are considering establishing requirements for Environmental Product Declarations (“EPDs”) to evaluate environmental impacts of products. California has enacted the “Buy Clean California Act” and California has established Global Warming Potential (GWP) benchmarks through EPDs for certain materials, including certain steel products.  Currently, the federal government is considering similar legislation. To provide for greater product transparency, Nucor contracted an independent, third-party to evaluate and publish EPDs for many of its products.  Nucor’s EPDs extend beyond what is required under the “Buy Clean California Act”, which requires EPDs for four steel products.  The following Nucor products have been evaluated and issued a corresponding EPD: fabricated hot-rolled structural steel sections; fabricated steel concrete reinforcing bar and merchant bar products; steel reinforcing bar and merchant bar products; fabricated steel hollow structural sections; fabricated structural plate; fabricated open web steel joist and joist girders; and fabricated steel roof and floor deck. EPD legislation has the potential to put domestic steel manufacturers at a disadvantage to foreign competitors unless standardized mechanisms are used to fully evaluate products produced by foreign steel producers.

Energy and fuel costs can fluctuate dramatically and, at times, have resulted in significant cost increases, particularly for the price of oil and gasoline. An increase in the price of oil increases our transportation costs for distribution, utility costs for our retail stores and costs to purchase our products from suppliers. Suriname has experienced political instability and uncertainty in the past which may continue in future years. General Risk Factors
Applicable laws and our certificate of incorporation and by-laws may delay, defer, prevent or render more difficult a takeover attempt that our stockholders might consider to be in their best interests. For example, Section 203 of the General Corporation Law of the State of Delaware may limit the ability of an “interested stockholder” to engage in business combinations with us. An interested stockholder is defined to include persons owning 15% or more of our outstanding voting stock. These provisions may make it difficult for stockholders to replace or remove our directors, which could delay, defer or prevent a change in control. Such provisions may prevent our stockholders from receiving the benefit from any premium to the market price of our common stock offered by a bidder in a takeover context. Even in the absence of a takeover attempt, the existence of these provisions may adversely affect the prevailing market price of our common stock if they are viewed as discouraging future takeover attempts. Additionally, applicable state and foreign insurance laws may require prior approval of an application to acquire control of a domestic insurer. State statutes generally provide, and certain foreign statutes provide, that control over a domestic insurer is presumed to exist when any person directly or indirectly owns, controls, has voting power over, or holds proxies representing, 10% or more of the domestic insurer’s voting securities. The application process can be extensive, thereby discouraging the acquisition of a control position. Our certificate of incorporation or by-laws contain provisions that permit the Board to issue one or more series of preferred stock, prohibit stockholders from filling vacancies on the Board, prohibit stockholders from calling special meetings of stockholders and from taking action by written consent and impose advance notice requirements for stockholder proposals and nominations of directors to be considered at stockholder meetings.

It also references board authority to issue preferred stock and advance notice requirements for nominations and proposals. These topics are directly about control, board structure, and shareholder rights, which are core elements of Corporate Governance. It does not primarily address business ethics misconduct, climate, labor, or other ESG categories.

Since COVID-19 was declared a global pandemic by the World Health Organization, our business, operations and financial performance have been, and may continue to be, affected by the macroeconomic impacts resulting from the efforts to control the spread of COVID-19. As a result of the scale of the ongoing pandemic, including the introduction of new variants of COVID-19 and vaccination and other efforts to control the spread, our revenue growth rate and expenses as a percentage of our revenues in future periods may differ significantly from our historical rates, and our future operating results may fall below expectations. Additionally, we may experience a significant and prolonged shift in user behavior such as a shift in interests to less commercial topics. As a result of the pandemic, our workforce shifted to operating in a primarily remote working environment, which continues to create inherent productivity, connectivity, and oversight challenges. The effects of the ongoing pandemic are dynamic and uneven. As we prepare to return our workforce in more locations back to the office, we may experience increased costs and/or disruption as we experiment with hybrid work models, in addition to potential effects on our ability to operate effectively and maintain our corporate culture.
label: Human Capital
reasoning: The paragraph explains that the shift to a remote working environment during COVID-19 creates productivity, connectivity, and oversight challenges, and it discusses returning to offices with potential disruption and increased costs. These concerns are directly tied to how workforce work arrangements affect performance and corporate culture. While the trigger is the pandemic, the specific risk articulated is workforce productivity and operational functioning under changing work models, making it Human Capital. It is not primarily about climate, pollution, waste, or governance structures.

BUSINESS RISKS
Our success depends upon the continued contributions of our associates. Our associates are the driving force behind our success. We believe that one of the things that distinguishes CarMax is a culture centered on valuing our associates. A failure to maintain our culture, in response to COVID-19 or in response to some other crisis, could have a material adverse effect on our business, sales and results of operations. In addition, managing our response to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic as well as our strategic initiatives require management, employees and contractors to adapt and learn new skills and capabilities. A failure to maintain an adaptable and responsive culture or to continue developing and retaining the associates that drive our success could have a material adverse effect on our business, sales and results of operations. The spread of COVID-19, especially in the early half of fiscal 2021, caused us to modify our business practices, including adopting measures such as hiring freezes, employee furloughs and reduction in pay for certain officers. We have subsequently lifted these measures, but as the pandemic continues or potentially worsens, we may have to adopt similar measures in the future that may affect our ability to maintain positive associate relations. If we are unable to maintain positive relations, or if, despite our efforts, we become subject to successful unionization efforts, it could increase costs, limit our ability to respond to competitive threats and have a material adverse effect on our business, sales and results of operations. Our response to COVID-19 and our ongoing success also depend upon the continued contributions of our store, region and corporate management teams. Consequently, the loss of the services of any of these associates could have a material adverse effect on our business, sales and results of operations.
label: Human Capital
reasoning: The paragraph centers on maintaining a culture that values associates and the risk that failing to maintain that culture in response to COVID-19 or other crises could materially affect business results. It also references workforce management actions such as hiring freezes, employee furloughs, and reduction in pay, and it warns about successful unionization efforts increasing costs and limiting responsiveness. The focus is clearly on employee relations, retention, culture, and workforce adjustments, which are core Human Capital themes. There is no substantial discussion of environmental impacts, waste, or product liability.

Legal and Regulatory Risks
We currently have approximately 1,450 employees who are represented by unions and covered by collective bargaining agreements and approximately 18,950 employees who are not represented by unions. Various unions occasionally seek to organize certain of our nonunion employees. Union organizing efforts or collective bargaining negotiations could potentially lead to work stoppages and/or slowdowns or strikes by certain of our employees, which could adversely affect our ability to serve our customers. Further, settlement of actual or threatened labor disputes or an increase in the number of our employees covered by collective bargaining agreements can have unknown effects on our labor costs, productivity and flexibility.  Under the collective bargaining agreements that we have signed, we are obligated to contribute to several multiemployer pension plans on behalf of some of our unionized employees. A multiemployer pension plan is a plan that covers the union-represented workers of various unrelated companies. Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, a contributing employer to an underfunded multiemployer plan is liable, generally upon withdrawal from a plan, for its proportionate share of the plan's unfunded vested liability. We currently have no intention of withdrawing from any multiemployer plan. However, there can be no assurance that we will not withdraw from one or more multiemployer plans in the future and be required to pay material amounts of withdrawal liability if one or more of those plans are underfunded at the time of withdrawal.
label: Human Capital
reasoning: The paragraph discusses risks from union organizing efforts and collective bargaining negotiations that could cause work stoppages, slowdowns, or strikes. It also addresses labor cost and productivity impacts from settlement or expansion of collective bargaining coverage and describes obligations tied to multiemployer pension plans for unionized employees. These are fundamentally Human Capital issues related to labor relations, workforce disruption, and employee benefit plan liabilities. The focus is not on environmental impacts or pollution, and it does not primarily concern governance of shareholders or product safety.

Strategy and Operational Risks
In November 2021, OSHA announced an Emergency Temporary Standard (“ETS”) mandating either full vaccination against COVID-19 or weekly testing of employees for employers with 100 or more employees; however, the agency withdrew the ETS in January 2022 following an unfavorable decision by the U.S. Supreme Court. OSHA has indicated that it will continue to pursue the vaccine and testing requirements of the ETS through the traditional rulemaking process, and additional vaccine mandates may be announced in jurisdictions in which our businesses operate. We cannot currently predict the impact of any such vaccine requirements on our workforce, although implementation may result in our inability to perform or compete for certain contracts, as well as significant cost, operational disruption, attrition and difficulty securing future labor needs in the already-constrained labor market. Market disruption, including labor shortages and supply chain constraints, and macroeconomic pressures, including the heightened pace of inflation, have adversely impacted our business and results of operations. Certain macroeconomic pressures and market disruption, driven in part by the COVID-19 pandemic, intensified during the second half of 2021 and are continuing. The constrained labor market has resulted in increased costs for wage adjustments, overtime hours and training new hires to address operational challenges servicing customers. The COVID-19 pandemic and the constrained labor market have also contributed to significant global supply chain disruption and inflationary pressure for the goods and services we purchase, with a particular impact on our repair and maintenance costs. Supply chain constraints have also caused delayed delivery of fleet, steel containers and other purchases. Aspects of our business rely on third-party transportation providers, and such services have become more limited and expensive.

It also links market disruption to labor shortages, wage and training pressures for new hires, and operational constraints in a constrained labor market. combined_text:
Cybersecurity Risk Management and Strategy
The Company’s mandatory annual cybersecurity employee training program covers critical aspects of digital security, including phishing prevention, threat awareness and safe data handling practices. The annual training program is regularly refreshed based on the evolving security landscape and secure code development. It is also supplemented by awareness initiatives to keep Company personnel updated on cybersecurity threats and the latest security policies and instill a culture of security mindfulness across the organization. •Continuous Review. The Company regularly reviews its cybersecurity policies, standards, and programs and evaluates the effectiveness of implemented security controls. In addition to performing internal audits, assessments, tabletop exercises, and vulnerability testing, the Company periodically engages third parties to perform information security maturity assessments, audits, cyber breach root cause analysis, and independent reviews of its information security control environment and operating effectiveness. The Company’s CISO provides regular reports on the results of such assessments to the Audit Committee and the Company’s senior leadership team, and the Company adjusts its cybersecurity policies, standards, and programs as necessary based on these reviews. To date, no risks from cybersecurity threats, including those resulting from any previous cybersecurity incidents, have  materially adversely affected, or are reasonably likely to materially adversely affect, the Company, including its business strategy, results of operations or financial condition. Although the Company’s cybersecurity risk management program, as described above, is designed to help prevent, detect, respond to, and mitigate the impact of cybersecurity incidents, there is no guarantee that a future cybersecurity incident would not materially adversely affect the Company's business strategy, results of operations or financial condition.
label: Natural Capital
reasoning: The text is about cybersecurity employee training, phishing prevention, threat awareness, safe data handling, and ongoing reviews and audits of security controls, including engagement of third parties and reporting to the Audit Committee. This is a risk related to digital security and information security management rather than environmental or workforce issues like emissions or labor health and safety. Because none of the described content concerns climate, water/biodiversity, pollution/waste, or traditional human capital topics, the closest fit is Product Liability through the inclusion of cybersecurity risk. It is also not Corporate Governance because the governance role is secondary to the core cybersecurity risk management practices.

combined_text:
Ameren Illinois expects to use the IEIMA performance-based formula ratemaking framework to establish annual customer rates effective through 2023. Effective for rates beginning in 2024, Ameren Illinois will establish electric distribution rates through either a traditional regulatory rate review or an MYRP. As a result of its participation in the IEIMA performance-based formula ratemaking, Ameren Illinois’ ROE for its electric distribution service through 2023 and its electric energy-efficiency investments is directly correlated to yields on United States Treasury bonds. Additionally, Ameren Illinois is subject to certain performance standards.  With respect to its natural gas delivery service business, unless extended, Ameren Illinois’ QIP will expire after December 2023.
With respect to the MYRP, the ICC-determined ROE would be subject to annual adjustments during the four-year period based on certain performance metrics, with aggregate symmetrical performance-based ROE incentives and penalties ranging from 20 to 60 basis points annually. While the ICC has approved a plan for Ameren Illinois to invest approximately $100 million per year in electric energy-efficiency programs through 2025, the ICC has the ability to reduce the amount of electric energy-efficiency savings goals in the future plan program years if there are insufficient cost-effective programs available, which could reduce the investments in electric energy-efficiency programs. The QIP provides Ameren Illinois with recovery of, and a return on, qualifying natural gas infrastructure investments that are placed in service between regulatory rate reviews. Infrastructure investments under the QIP earn a return at the applicable WACC. Ameren Illinois’ QIP is subject to a rate impact limitation of a cumulative 4% per year since the most recent delivery service rate order, with no single year exceeding 5.5%. If the rate impact limitation was met in a particular year, the amount of rate base causing the QIP rate to exceed the limitation would be exposed to regulatory lag until a year when that amount could be recovered under QIP or is added to rate base as a part of a regulatory rate review. Upon issuance of a natural gas delivery service rate order, QIP rate base is transferred to base rates and the QIP is reset to zero. Without legislative action, the QIP will expire after December 2023.
label: Non-ESG
reasoning: The paragraph focuses on rate-setting mechanisms, regulatory frameworks, performance metrics, and potential reductions in investment in electric energy-efficiency programs, along with the timing and recovery of costs and returns. Although it references electric energy-efficiency investments, it is framed as regulatory and financial rate recovery risk rather than describing environmental outcomes like emissions reductions or pollution controls. There is no explicit discussion of climate transition, decarbonization targets, water stress, biodiversity, or waste. Therefore, the correct classification is Non-ESG because the core risk is regulatory/financial incentives and possible investment reductions due to regulatory decisions.

Risks Related to Our Business
The U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (the “FCPA”) and similar foreign anti-corruption laws in other jurisdictions around the world generally prohibit companies and their intermediaries from making improper payments or providing anything of value to non-U.S. government officials for the purpose of obtaining or retaining business or securing an unfair advantage. Although we have established formal policies or procedures for prohibiting or monitoring this conduct, we cannot assure you that our employees or other agents will not engage in such conduct for which we might be held responsible. In the event that we believe or have reason to believe that our employees, agents or distributors have or may have violated applicable anti-corruption laws, including the FCPA, we may be required to investigate or have outside counsel investigate the relevant facts and circumstances, which can be expensive and require significant time and attention from senior management. LEGAL RISKS.
The FCPA, the U.K. Bribery Act of 2010 (“UKBA”), and similar anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws in other jurisdictions generally prohibit companies from offering and making corrupt payments to or otherwise engaging in bribery of government officials. Because of the predominance of government-sponsored healthcare systems around the world, many of our customer relationships outside of the United States are with governmental entities, the employees of which may be considered government officials under such laws. Many anti-corruption laws, such as the UKBA, also prohibit bribery of private sector individuals, and thus extend far beyond interactions with government officials. We also are subject to the FCPA’s accounting provisions, which require us to keep accurate books and records and to maintain an adequate system of internal accounting controls sufficient to provide reasonable assurances of management’s control, authority, and responsibility over our assets. Non-U.S. companies, including some of our competitors, may not be subject to the provisions of the FCPA. If these competitors engage in corrupt practices, they may gain a business advantage. Global enforcement of anti-corruption laws has increased substantially in recent years, with more frequent voluntary self-disclosure by companies, aggressive investigations (including coordinated investigations across countries and governmental authorities) and enforcement proceedings by U.S. and non-U.S. governmental agencies, and assessment of significant civil and criminal fines, penalties, and other sanctions against companies and individuals. Companies in the healthcare sector have been a particular focus of government enforcement in recent years.

In addition, other applicable anti-corruption laws prohibit bribery of domestic government officials, and some laws that may apply to our operations prohibit commercial bribery, including giving or receiving improper payments to or from non-government parties, as well as so-called “facilitation” payments. In addition, we are subject to U.S. and other applicable trade control regulations that restrict with whom we may transact business, including the trade sanctions enforced by the U.S. Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control. If we fail to comply with laws and regulations restricting dealings with sanctioned countries or companies and/or persons on restricted lists, we may be subject to civil or criminal penalties. Any future violations could have an adverse impact on our ability to sell our products to United States federal, state and local government and related entities. We have business relationships with companies in China who have been, or may in the future be, added to the restricted party list.

We have two classes of common equity: our Common Stock and our Class A Common Stock. The holders of Common Stock currently are entitled, as a class, to elect only one-third of our Board of Directors. This ownership position may increase if other members of the Smith Family enter into the voting trust agreement, and the voting power relating to this ownership position may increase if shares of our Class A Common Stock held by stockholders who are not parties to the voting trust agreement are converted into shares of our Common Stock.

We are controlled by the MD stockholders, who, together with the SLP stockholders, collectively own a substantial majority of our common stock and are able to effectively control our actions, including approval of mergers and other significant corporate transactions.

Through their control, the MD stockholders are able to control our actions, including actions related to the election of our directors and directors of our subsidiaries (including VMware, Inc. and its subsidiaries), amendments to our organizational documents, and the approval of significant corporate transactions, including mergers and sales of substantially all of our assets that our stockholders may deem advantageous. Further, as of January 29, 2021, the MD stockholders and the SLP stockholders collectively beneficially owned 65.2% of our outstanding common stock. Interested Directors.
Bermuda law and Group’s bye-laws provide that if a director has a personal interest in a transaction to which the company is also a party and if the director discloses the nature of this personal interest at the first opportunity, either at a meeting of directors or in writing to the directors, then the company will not be able to declare the transaction void solely due to the existence of that personal interest and the director will not be liable to the company for any profit realized from the transaction. In addition, after a director has made the declaration of interest referred to above, he or she is allowed to be counted for purposes of determining whether a quorum is present and to vote on a transaction in which he or she has an interest, unless disqualified from doing so by the chairman of the relevant board meeting. Under Delaware law, an interested director could be held liable for a transaction in which that director derived an improper personal benefit. Additionally, under Delaware law, a corporation may be able to declare a transaction with an interested director to be void unless one of the following conditions is fulfilled:•the material facts as to the interested director’s relationship or interests are disclosed or are known to the board of directors and the board in good faith authorizes the transaction by the affirmative vote of a majority of the disinterested directors;•the material facts are disclosed or are known to the shareholders entitled to vote on the transaction and the transaction is specifically approved in good faith by the holders of a majority of the voting shares; or•the transaction is fair to the corporation as of the time it is authorized, approved or ratified.

It also covers governance mechanics such as whether an interested director can be counted for quorum and vote on the transaction unless disqualified. The paragraph further outlines Delaware law conditions for approving or voiding transactions involving interested directors, focusing on fiduciary/transaction approval governance concepts. This is squarely about internal governance and conflict-of-interest handling rather than ESG environmental, labor, or product issues.

LEGAL, REGULATORY AND PUBLIC POLICY RISKS
Our articles of incorporation provide that no person may beneficially own shares of voting capital stock in excess of specified ownership limits, except with the prior approval of a majority of the “continuing directors.” The ownership limits, which may not be exceeded without the prior approval of the BCBSA, are the following: (1) for any institutional investor (as defined in our articles of incorporation), one share less than 10% of our outstanding voting securities; (2) for any non-institutional investor (as defined in our articles of incorporation), one share less than 5% of our outstanding voting securities; and (3) for any person, one share less than the number of shares of our common stock or other equity securities (or a combination thereof) representing a 20% ownership interest in us. In addition, our articles of incorporation and bylaws: divide our Board of Directors into three classes serving staggered three-year terms (which is required by our license agreement with the BCBSA); permit our Board of Directors to determine the terms of and issue one or more series of preferred stock without further action by shareholders; restrict the maximum number of directors and the ability to increase that number; limit the ability of shareholders to remove directors; impose restrictions on shareholders’ ability to fill vacancies on our Board of Directors; impose advance notice requirements for shareholder proposals and nominations of directors to be considered at meetings of shareholders; prohibit shareholders from amending certain provisions of our bylaws; and impose restrictions on who may call a special meeting of shareholders.
label: Corporate Governance
reasoning: This paragraph lists governance and charter/bylaw provisions that constrain share ownership limits, stagger board terms into classes, and limit shareholder rights to remove directors, fill vacancies, call meetings, and amend certain bylaws. It also describes preferred stock issuance authority and advance notice requirements for nominations and proposals, all of which are classic corporate control and shareholder rights governance features. Natural capital, pollution, and product-related categories are not appropriate because the text is focused on corporate governance structure under articles of incorporation and bylaws.

Under the Maryland General Corporation Law, certain "business combinations" between a Maryland corporation and an interested stockholder or an affiliate of an interested stockholder are prohibited for five years after the most recent date on which the interested stockholder becomes an interested stockholder. Section 203, subject to certain exceptions, prohibits a Delaware corporation from engaging in any “business combination” with any “interested stockholder” for a period of three years following the date that such stockholder became an interested stockholder unless:•prior to such date, the board of directors of the corporation approved either the business combination or the transaction that resulted in the stockholder becoming an interested stockholder;•upon consummation of the transaction that resulted in the stockholder becoming an interested stockholder, the interested stockholder owned at least 85% of the voting stock of the corporation outstanding at the time the transaction commenced, excluding those shares owned by persons who are directors and also officers, and employee stock plans in which employee participants do not have the right to determine confidentially whether shares held subject to the plan will be tendered in a tender or exchange offer; or•on or subsequent to such date, the business combination is approved by the board of directors and authorized at an annual or special meeting of stockholders, and not by written consent, by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the outstanding voting stock that is not owned by the interested stockholder. In general, Section 203 defines “business combination” to include mergers or consolidations between a Delaware corporation and an interested stockholder, transactions with an interested stockholder involving the assets or stock of the corporation or its majority-owned subsidiaries and transactions which increase an interested stockholder’s percentage ownership of stock. In general, Section 203 defines an “interested stockholder” as any entity or person beneficially owning 15% or more of the outstanding voting stock of the corporation and any entity or person affiliated with or controlling or controlled by such entity or person.

Risks Related to Ownership of our Common Stock
The Company's charter, bylaws and Maryland law contain provisions that could make it more difficult for a third party to acquire the Company without the consent of our Board. Risks Related to Our Industry and Business Operations
Our ability to meet the existing and future demand of our customers depends on the availability of an adequate supply of water. As a general rule, sources of public water supply, including rivers, lakes, streams, groundwater aquifers and recycled water sources, are held in the public trust and are not generally owned by private interests. As a result, we typically do not own the source water that we use in our operations, and the availability of our water supply is established through allocation rights (determined by legislation or court decisions) and passing-flow requirements set by governmental entities or by entering into water purchase agreements. These requirements, which can change from time to time, and vary by state or region, may adversely impact our water supply. Supply issues, such as drought, overuse of sources of water, the protection of threatened species or habitats, contamination or other factors may limit the availability of ground and surface water. If we are unable to secure available or alternative sources of water, our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows could be adversely affected. For example, in our Monterey County, California operations, we are seeking to augment our sources of water supply, principally to comply with an October 2009 cease and desist order (the “2009 Order”), as amended by a July 2016 order (the “2016 Order”), of the SWRCB that requires our California subsidiary to significantly decrease its diversions from the Carmel River in accordance with a reduction schedule that terminated on December 31, 2021 (the “2021 Deadline”). See Item 3—Legal Proceedings—Alternative Water Supply in Lieu of Carmel River Diversions, which includes additional information regarding this matter. We are also required to augment our Monterey County sources of water supply to comply with the requirements of the Endangered Species Act.
label: Natural Capital
reasoning: This paragraph is centered on the availability of adequate water supply for operations and the risks associated with water scarcity. It describes how water supply depends on allocation rights, passing-flow requirements, water purchase agreements, and how changing legal or regulatory requirements can adversely impact water supply. Risks Related to our Company and Operations
Quality water is a key ingredient in our brewing process. Clean water is a limited resource in many parts of the world and climate change may increase water scarcity and cause a deterioration of water quality in areas where we maintain brewing operations. The competition for water among domestic, agricultural and manufacturing users is increasing in some of our brewing communities and communities in which we or our suppliers manufacture our other products. Even where water is widely available, water purification and waste treatment infrastructure limitations could increase costs or constrain our operations. Further, unavailability of clean water at our breweries or our other facilities or the facilities of our suppliers could limit our ability to brew, which could cause a decrease in production. We have substantial brewery operations in the states of Colorado and Texas, which have been areas vulnerable to water scarcity conditions. Certain western states in the U.S. are experiencing an extended drought, which can impact the quality and quantity of agricultural ingredients such as barley and hops. The continuation or recurrence of such conditions could have an adverse effect upon our agricultural supply chain. We and our suppliers are dependent on sufficient amounts of quality water for operation of our breweries and key facilities and the key facilities of our significant suppliers. The suppliers of the agricultural raw materials we purchase are also dependent upon sufficient supplies of quality water for their fields. A substantial reduction in water in certain agricultural areas could result in material losses of crops, such as barley or hops, which could lead to a shortage of our product supply. If water available to our operations or the operations of our suppliers becomes scarce or the quality of that water deteriorates, we may incur increased production costs or face production constraints, which could adversely affect our business and financial results.
label: Natural Capital
reasoning: This paragraph explicitly links clean water scarcity and deteriorating water quality to operational constraints in brewing, noting that clean water is limited and that climate change may worsen water scarcity. It also describes competition for water among users and infrastructure limitations that affect purification and waste treatment, but the dominant risk is loss of access to sufficient quality water and resulting production constraints. Additionally, drought is tied to reduced quality and quantity of agricultural inputs like barley and hops, affecting the agricultural supply chain. These are characteristic Natural Capital concerns about water stress and impacts to natural resource-dependent ingredients, while it is not primarily Pollution & Waste or Product Liability.

Given the nature of our business, we, together with our third-party business partners, receive, collect, process, use, and retain sensitive and confidential customer, patient, and employee data, in addition to proprietary business information. Some of our third-party business partners, such as identity verification and payment processing providers, also regularly have access to customer data. Additionally, we maintain other confidential, proprietary, or otherwise sensitive information relating to our business and from third parties. Global privacy, cybersecurity and data protection-related laws and regulations are evolving, extensive, and complex. Compliance with these laws and regulations is challenging and costly. The interpretation and application of these laws in some instances is uncertain, and our legal and regulatory obligations are subject to frequent changes. We are required to comply with increasingly complex and changing data privacy regulations both in the United States and beyond that regulate the collection, use, security, processing, and transfer of personal data, including particularly the transfer of personal data between or among countries. Many of these regulations also grant rights to individuals. We collect and store confidential, personal information relating to our customers for various business purposes, including marketing and financial purposes, and credit card information for processing payments. For example, we handle, collect and store personal information in connection with our customers staying at our hotels and enrolling in Caesars Rewards. It also notes that systems used for payment card transactions and payment card technology can put payment card data at risk, and that some systems are controlled by the payment card industry. Product Liability is appropriate because these statements describe security and data-protection risks embedded in the company’s information systems and services. It is not Pollution & Waste or Natural Capital since there is no discussion of environmental resources or waste streams.

Risks Related to Our Industry, Customers, Products and Services
Our FortiGuard and other security subscription services may falsely detect, report and act on viruses or other threats that do not actually exist. This risk is heightened by the inclusion of a “heuristics” feature in our products, which attempts to identify viruses and other threats not based on any known signatures but based on characteristics or anomalies that may indicate that a particular item is a threat. When our end-customers enable the heuristics feature in our products, the risk of falsely identifying viruses and other threats significantly increases. These false positives, while typical in the industry, may impair the perceived reliability of our products and may therefore adversely impact market acceptance of our products. Also, our FortiGuard and other security subscription services may falsely identify emails or programs as unwanted spam or potentially unwanted programs, or alternatively fail to properly identify unwanted emails or programs, particularly as spam emails or spyware are often designed to circumvent anti-spam or spyware products. Parties whose emails or programs are blocked by our products may seek redress against us for labeling them as spammers or spyware, or for interfering with their business. In addition, false identification of emails or programs as unwanted spam or potentially unwanted programs may reduce the adoption of our products. If our system restricts important files or applications based on falsely identifying them as malware or some other item that should be restricted, this could adversely affect end-customers’ systems and cause material system failures. In addition, our threat researchers periodically identify vulnerabilities in various third-party products, and, if these identifications are perceived to be incorrect or are in fact incorrect, this could harm our business.

(2) laws imposing obligations on businesses that collect or disclose biometric information (including, in Colorado, Illinois, Texas, and Washington); (3) laws governing the collection and processing of children and minor's data and how companies provide age-appropriate online experiences (including, in the US, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998; and (4) laws regulating internet-connected devices (such as, in California, the Internet of Things Security Law).•The EU's Digital Markets Act, which requires in-scope companies to obtain user consent for combining data across certain products and require search engines to share anonymized data with rival companies, among other changes; and the EU Data Act, which introduces new data portability requirements with respect to connected products (i.e., 'internet of things' products) and related services, as well as interoperability obligations on data processing services.

reasoning: This paragraph supports the Product Liability label because it discusses regulatory obligations that affect the company’s product and service privacy practices, specifically the processing and security of personal data. It cites the EU GDPR/UK GDPR applicability and then details US and foreign privacy laws, including data breach exposure where reasonable security procedures and practices are required. It also highlights laws governing children and minors’ data and age-appropriate online experiences, as well as biometric data rules and security requirements for internet-connected devices. The focus is on how the company must design and operate its products to manage privacy and data security risk, not on environmental or labor issues, making Product Liability the best match among the provided categories.

Operational Risks Related to our Business
If our electronic data is compromised our business could be significantly harmed. We and our business partners maintain significant amounts of data electronically in locations around the world and in the cloud. This data relates to all aspects of our business, including current and future products and entertainment under development, and also contains certain customer, consumer, supplier, partner and employee data. We maintain systems and processes designed to protect this data, but notwithstanding such protective measures, there is a risk of intrusion, cyber-attacks or tampering that could compromise the integrity and privacy of this data. Cyber-attacks are increasing in their frequency, sophistication and intensity, and are becoming increasingly difficult to detect. They are often carried out by motivated, well-resourced, skilled and persistent actors, including nation states, organized crime groups, “hacktivists” and employees or contractors acting with malicious intent. Cyber-attacks could include the deployment of harmful malware and key loggers, ransomware, a denial-of-service attack, a malicious website, the use of social engineering and other means to affect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of our technology systems and data. Cyber-attacks could also include supply chain attacks, which could cause a delay in the manufacturing of our products. In addition, we provide confidential and proprietary information to our third-party business partners in certain cases where doing so is necessary to conduct our business. While we obtain assurances from those parties that they have systems and processes in place to protect such data, and where applicable, that they will take steps to assure the protections of such data by third parties, those partners may also be subject to data intrusion or otherwise compromise the protection of such data.
label: Product Liability
reasoning: The gold label Product Liability fits because the paragraph focuses on cybersecurity and data integrity/privacy risks involving electronic data stored in the cloud and across business systems, including customer and employee data. It discusses risks of intrusion, cyber-attacks, tampering, and specific attack vectors like malware, ransomware, key loggers, and denial-of-service, all of which relate to the protection of data handled through the company’s technology products and services. It also notes that cyber-attacks could cause supply chain delays affecting products, further linking the risk to product delivery and technology operations. Environmental and social ESG categories are not the main subject; the dominant theme is privacy/security incident risk that can lead to liability exposure, consistent with Product Liability’s inclusion of cybersecurity and privacy and data protection.

We continue to be the target of attempted cybersecurity and other threats that could have a security impact, including those by third parties to access, misappropriate, corrupt or manipulate our information or disrupt our operations. We expect to continue to experience an increase in cybersecurity threats in the future, as the volume and intensity of cyberattacks on hospitals, health systems and other health care entities continue to increase.

Risks Related to Employee and Contractor Compliance with Code of Conduct
We are subject to laws and regulations governing business conduct, including requirements related to workplace ethics, accuracy of business records, and restrictions on improper payments. Our employees and contractors are expected to comply with our code of conduct and related policies, including those addressing conflicts of interest, gifts and entertainment, recordkeeping, and fair dealing. We also rely on periodic training and certifications to reinforce expectations.

However, compliance is not always within our direct control, especially for contractors working at customer sites or on behalf of us. Pressure to meet commercial goals, misunderstandings of policy requirements, insufficient supervision, or inadequate training can lead to violations. In addition, changes in processes or systems may temporarily create uncertainty around documentation or approval steps.

If we experience misconduct or noncompliance, we could face civil and criminal penalties, termination of certain relationships, and restrictions on our ability to bid for contracts. We may need to conduct internal investigations, implement remediation plans, and strengthen oversight and monitoring. Any such actions could be costly and may divert management resources. Moreover, negative publicity from alleged ethics violations can impair our ability to recruit employees and maintain customer and investor confidence.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: The label is appropriate because the paragraph addresses employee and contractor compliance with a code of conduct, including recordkeeping accuracy, restrictions on improper payments, conflicts of interest, gifts and entertainment, and fair dealing. It explains that compliance failures can occur due to pressure to meet commercial goals, misunderstandings, insufficient supervision, or inadequate training. Potential outcomes—civil and criminal penalties, termination of relationships, internal investigations, remediation, and negative publicity—are classic Business Ethics & Values risks rather than climate, pollution, or product liability.

combined_text:
Political Contributions, Lobbying Practices and Regulatory Scrutiny
We engage in activities intended to inform policymakers and regulators about our business and industry matters, including through public policy statements, participation in industry associations, and, where permitted, political contributions and lobbying-related expenditures. These activities are subject to a complex set of laws and regulations, including rules governing political contributions, disclosure, reporting, and restrictions on gifts or compensation. The legal and regulatory requirements can vary by jurisdiction and may change over time.

Our policies are designed to ensure that any political or lobbying activity is authorized and properly documented. Nonetheless, mistakes in tracking approvals, insufficient documentation, or misunderstanding of local requirements could result in reporting errors or allegations that expenditures were not properly authorized. In addition, third parties that support lobbying or grassroots efforts may fail to follow our contractual requirements.

If regulators conclude that our political or lobbying practices violate applicable law or are designed to improperly influence public officials, we could face fines, enforcement actions, negative publicity, and limitations on future political activity. In some cases, alleged violations may also lead to shareholder claims that we failed in our oversight responsibilities. Even without an adverse legal outcome, inquiries can consume management time and require significant compliance spend.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: This paragraph is correctly categorized as Business Ethics & Values because it focuses on political contributions and lobbying practices, including compliance with laws governing contributions, disclosure, gifts, and proper authorization. It describes risks from tracking approval mistakes, insufficient documentation, and third parties failing to follow contractual requirements, leading to allegations that expenditures were not properly authorized or improperly intended to influence public officials. The consequences listed—fines, enforcement actions, negative publicity, and potential shareholder claims regarding oversight—are ethics and regulatory conduct concerns, not an environmental or social category.

combined_text:
Risks of Noncompliance with Securities Laws and Disclosure Controls
We depend on accurate and timely financial reporting and disclosures to support investor confidence. We are subject to U.S. and international securities laws that prohibit insider trading, market manipulation, and false or misleading statements in public filings. While we maintain disclosure controls and procedures and an insider trading policy, risks remain that individuals may trade securities while possessing material nonpublic information, communicate nonpublic information inappropriately, or fail to follow reporting procedures.

Additionally, our reporting may be affected by changes to accounting standards, complex estimates, or incomplete data feeds from operational systems. If our internal controls are not sufficient to prevent or detect errors, we may issue inaccurate disclosures. Correction of disclosure issues could involve restatements, regulatory inquiries, enforcement actions, and litigation by investors.

We also face risk of allegations that our guidance, marketing materials, or other public statements were misleading. Such allegations may arise during market downturns or following disappointing operating results, even if the statements were made in good faith and based on available information at the time.

Any investigation or litigation could require substantial time and expense and could distract management from executing our strategy.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: The gold label is correct because this paragraph is about noncompliance with securities laws and disclosure controls, including insider trading, market manipulation, and false or misleading statements in public filings. It also describes risks of individuals trading with material nonpublic information, improper communication of nonpublic information, and failure of internal controls leading to inaccurate disclosures or restatements. Although it discusses disclosure systems, the underlying issue is ethical/legal compliance in financial reporting and market conduct, making other ESG categories or Non-ESG less plausible.

combined_text:
Failure to Detect and Remediate Ethical Issues in Acquired Businesses
We may acquire companies, assets, or technology and integrate their operations into ours. Acquisitions can introduce legacy practices, systems, and relationships that may not meet our ethical and compliance standards at the time of acquisition. While we conduct due diligence, that diligence may not identify all instances of improper conduct, inadequate controls, or undisclosed disputes. Some issues may relate to prior sales practices, pricing and billing, customer communications, procurement, or the conduct of agents and intermediaries.

If ethical issues are discovered after closing, we could incur expenses to remediate noncompliance, strengthen internal controls, and potentially renegotiate or terminate contracts. Certain matters could lead to regulatory inquiries, private lawsuits, or criminal or civil proceedings. Even when we believe we are not at fault, acquiring liability can occur for certain conduct that occurred before closing, including allegations that we failed to take sufficient corrective actions after integration.

The integration process may also create additional compliance risks. Employees may be unfamiliar with our policies, approval procedures, or reporting requirements. Systems integration can temporarily limit our ability to monitor transactions, increasing the risk that misconduct goes undetected.

These events may delay integration milestones, impair customer relationships, and adversely affect our operating results and reputation.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: This paragraph is labeled Business Ethics & Values because it focuses on ethical and compliance failures arising from acquisitions, including “improper conduct,” “inadequate controls,” and “undisclosed disputes.” It specifically discusses remediation for legacy practices that may not meet “ethical and compliance standards,” along with potential “regulatory inquiries,” “private lawsuits,” and “criminal or civil proceedings.” It also mentions integration-related monitoring gaps that increase the risk misconduct goes undetected, which is an internal control and ethical oversight theme. The alternative categories like Pollution & Waste, Natural Capital, and Climate Change are not implicated because the risks are centered on ethics, compliance, and governance in acquired operations.

Risks Related to Misuse of Corporate Assets and Improper Expenses
We have policies and procedures intended to ensure the appropriate use of company resources, including authorization of expenditures, expense reporting controls, and restrictions on personal use of assets. Despite these safeguards, employees may misuse corporate resources, submit improper expenses, or circumvent approval requirements. Examples could include charging personal travel, inflating vendor invoices, using corporate payment instruments for unauthorized transactions, or misrepresenting reimbursement documentation.

These issues may be more likely in periods of high travel, remote work, or changes to expense systems. Fraud risk can also increase when internal audit resources are constrained or when personnel turnover reduces institutional knowledge regarding compliance practices. Additionally, third-party administrators or travel platforms may introduce operational complexity and reduce the effectiveness of manual controls.

If misuse of corporate assets or expense reporting fraud is not detected promptly, we could face legal actions, disciplinary actions against employees, and potential losses. Misconduct may also trigger regulatory inquiries related to recordkeeping and internal controls, particularly if improper expenses are material to our financial statements. Reputational harm can result from public allegations of misconduct, even if such allegations do not lead to a final determination.

We may be required to implement additional monitoring tools, enhance training, or restructure internal control processes, which could increase costs and slow operational workflows.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: The gold label fits Business Ethics & Values because the text centers on fraud and misuse of corporate resources, including “misuse of corporate resources,” “submit improper expenses,” and “misrepresenting reimbursement documentation.” It ties these behaviors to “fraud risk,” “internal audit resources,” and the likelihood of legal, regulatory, and reputational consequences if misconduct is not detected. The paragraph also describes enhanced monitoring and training to strengthen internal controls, which is characteristic of ethical and compliance conduct risk. Natural Capital, Pollution & Waste, and Human Capital are not primary here because the subject is financial misconduct, expense reporting integrity, and governance of expenditures.

combined_text:
Risks from Inadequate Oversight of Third-Party Partners
A portion of our customer interactions and operations is performed by third-party partners, including resellers, fulfillment vendors, and customer support providers. We contractually require these partners to comply with applicable laws and our ethical standards, including requirements related to truthful marketing, accurate billing, and proper handling of customer communications. We also perform due diligence and ongoing monitoring.

However, third parties may not fully comply with contractual requirements due to differences in training, staffing, incentives, or local market practices. For example, resellers may misrepresent product capabilities, offer noncompliant pricing terms, or fail to maintain appropriate documentation. Customer support providers may improperly represent service commitments or fail to follow complaint handling procedures.

If partner conduct violates law or our standards, we may be subject to regulatory actions, consumer protection claims, and investigations into our oversight practices. While some partners could bear responsibility contractually, enforcement may not be practical or recovery of damages may be limited. In addition, issues caused by third parties can create customer dissatisfaction, increase chargebacks or refunds, and negatively affect brand reputation.

Our ability to detect issues depends on the quality of our reporting, audit rights, and monitoring data. If monitoring proves insufficient, misconduct could persist for longer periods and increase the magnitude of any resulting harm.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: This is correctly classified as Business Ethics & Values because it addresses improper or unethical conduct by third-party partners, including violations of “laws and our ethical standards” related to truthful marketing, accurate billing, and customer communications. The paragraph gives examples such as resellers “misrepresent[ing] product capabilities,” failing to maintain proper documentation, and customer support providers misrepresenting commitments or complaint handling. It further describes consequences like “regulatory actions,” “consumer protection claims,” and investigations into oversight practices, all rooted in ethical compliance supervision. Pollution, climate, and human-capital categories are not the main focus since the risk is about integrity of partner conduct and the adequacy of oversight.

Compliance Risks Related to Data Handling and Representations to Customers
We collect and process customer information in connection with our services. While our primary controls for data protection are described elsewhere, ethical and conduct-related obligations also arise regarding what we represent to customers about data use, consent, and retention. Our disclosures and contractual commitments must be consistent with actual practices. If we fail to follow our own stated privacy commitments or marketing representations, regulators may allege deceptive practices or unfair treatment, and customers may bring claims for breach of contract or violations of law.

Risks include errors in consent flows, incomplete configuration of data retention schedules, inadequate review of third-party tools used to process data, or internal misunderstandings regarding the scope of permissions granted by customers. Even if a technical issue is remediated, alleged misrepresentations may trigger investigations, remediation orders, and reputational harm.

In addition, employees may access customer data improperly for non-business reasons or may not follow internal documentation requirements for security exceptions. Such conduct could be viewed as violating ethical standards and governance processes. If any misconduct is discovered, we could face penalties, consent decrees, and increased compliance obligations.

Because regulators and courts may interpret disclosures broadly, we could be held responsible for how our disclosures are understood, even in cases where the underlying system did not operate exactly as intended.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: The paragraph matches Business Ethics & Values because it links data handling to ethical and conduct-related obligations, emphasizing consistency between “privacy commitments,” disclosures, and “marketing representations” versus actual practices. It warns that failure to follow stated commitments could lead regulators to allege “deceptive practices” or “unfair treatment,” and that customers may bring claims for breach of contract or violations of law. It also references improper employee access to customer data “for non-business reasons,” which is misconduct and governance-related rather than a purely technical privacy issue. Product Liability is a plausible alternative given data handling could involve service risks, but the dominant theme is ethical misrepresentation and compliance with commitments and oversight processes.

Risks Related to Employee Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Complaints
We are committed to providing a respectful and safe workplace. Our code of conduct and employment policies address discrimination, harassment, and retaliation, and we maintain reporting and investigation processes. Despite these measures, employees or supervisors may engage in behavior that violates policies or applicable law, whether through misconduct or failure to prevent and address inappropriate conduct. Complaints can also arise regarding inconsistent application of workplace policies, perceived favoritism, or unclear standards.

If we do not effectively prevent misconduct or handle complaints appropriately, we could face legal claims, including employment-related lawsuits, administrative actions by regulators, and payment of damages or settlements. Findings of wrongdoing can also lead to remedial actions and increased oversight by enforcement agencies. Even where allegations are ultimately unsubstantiated, defending claims can be time-consuming and costly and may negatively affect employee morale and retention.

Additionally, retaliation concerns may prompt whistleblowers or employees to avoid reporting issues, which can delay detection of ethical problems and prolong exposure to harm. Remote work and rapid organizational changes can further complicate management oversight and investigation timelines.

We cannot assure that our policies, training, investigations, and disciplinary actions will always be effective in preventing conduct or mitigating the impact of any alleged violations.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: This paragraph is correctly labeled Business Ethics & Values because it addresses discrimination, harassment, and retaliation complaints under a company code of conduct and employment policies. It discusses risks that employees or supervisors may violate policies or law, complaints tied to “favoritism” or inconsistent application, and the consequences of inadequate prevention or complaint handling such as “employment-related lawsuits,” “administrative actions,” and settlements. It also highlights ethical detection risk when “retaliation concerns” cause whistleblowers to avoid reporting, undermining misconduct detection. While Human Capital could seem relevant, the language is framed around ethical misconduct, retaliation, and compliance enforcement outcomes, making Business Ethics & Values the best fit.

combined_text:
Accuracy and Integrity Risks in Customer Billing and Collections Practices
Our revenue depends on accurate billing, pricing, and collection processes. We are required to follow applicable consumer protection, billing, and collection laws and to maintain truthful and transparent communications with customers. Inaccurate billing may result from system errors, incorrect configuration of contracts or rate plans, and manual adjustments that are not properly reviewed. Ethical risks can also arise when employees attempt to compensate for process problems by making inappropriate overrides or by failing to honor agreed contract terms.

If we do not maintain strong controls over billing changes, credits, waivers, and collections communications, we could face allegations of unfair or deceptive practices. Such allegations may lead to enforcement actions, class action litigation, refund obligations, and required changes to billing systems and customer scripts. Regulators may also impose consent decrees or require additional auditing and reporting.

Even when errors are inadvertent, investigations into the integrity of our processes can lead to scrutiny of how we design controls, how we document exceptions, and whether management oversight is adequate. Substantial penalties may be imposed in the event of material violations.

To manage these risks, we invest in process documentation and control testing; however, we cannot ensure that these measures will be sufficient to prevent future incidents or limit their impact.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: The gold label is appropriate because the paragraph focuses on integrity and ethics in billing and collections, including “unfair or deceptive practices” and compliance with consumer protection billing laws. It describes ethical risk where employees make “inappropriate overrides” or fail to honor contract terms, and it explains potential enforcement actions like “consent decrees,” class action litigation, refunds, and required changes to billing systems and scripts. The discussion of investigations into how controls and management oversight were designed and documented is consistent with ethical governance and internal controls rather than environmental topics. Product Liability is not the primary alternative because the risks are about commercial conduct and customer deception, not product safety or related liability.

combined_text:
Regulatory and Litigation Risks from Allegations of Unfair or Misleading Sales Practices
We rely on marketing and sales teams to communicate our offerings and to guide customers in selecting products and services. In certain industries, regulators and consumers may allege that sales practices are unfair, deceptive, or misleading if customers claim they were not adequately informed about key terms, fees, limitations, or eligibility criteria. Although we provide training and require use of standardized contract language and marketing materials, risks remain that individuals may deviate from approved scripts or present information in a manner that overstates benefits.

We also use lead-generation partners and advertising platforms that may provide targeting and performance metrics. Errors in attribution, referral agreements, or the messaging content used by partners can contribute to disputes regarding what was communicated to prospective customers. If we fail to promptly correct misleading communications, the issue can spread quickly and increase the likelihood of regulatory complaints.

Any investigation may require substantial cooperation and the production of large volumes of records, including internal emails and training materials. Adverse outcomes could include civil penalties, injunctions, rescission of contracts, restitution, and class action settlements. In addition, reputational damage could affect customer acquisition and retention.

We cannot assure that our controls and training will prevent all instances of miscommunication or improper sales conduct.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: This paragraph is labeled Business Ethics & Values because it describes regulatory and litigation risk from “unfair, deceptive, or misleading” sales practices and marketing communications. It explains that even with training and standardized materials, individuals may deviate from approved scripts or “overstate benefits,” and lead-generation partners can cause disputes about what was communicated. It also outlines consequences such as civil penalties, injunctions, rescission of contracts, restitution, and class action settlements, which are typical of conduct and misrepresentation allegations. Other ESG categories are unlikely since the central issue is ethical sales conduct and truthful communication with customers rather than environmental or labor impacts.

combined_text:
Whistleblower Allegations and Internal Investigation Exposure
We provide mechanisms for employees and other stakeholders to raise concerns through confidential reporting channels. These mechanisms are intended to facilitate early detection of misconduct, including fraud, improper accounting, and violations of law or our code of conduct. However, whistleblower complaints may be inaccurate, incomplete, or based on misunderstandings. Even when allegations are not substantiated, complaints can lead to internal investigations, regulator inquiries, and significant costs.

We are required to handle complaints consistently and to protect the confidentiality of reporters, while also meeting legal requirements. Investigations may uncover additional issues and may require changes to processes, personnel, or disclosures. In some cases, investigations could reveal weaknesses in our control environment or governance processes.

Employees may also allege retaliation if they believe they were treated adversely after reporting. Although we maintain anti-retaliation policies, proving the absence of retaliatory motives can be difficult. Such disputes can increase legal exposure and may require remedial measures.

Because the outcomes and timing of investigations are uncertain, we could be forced to recognize charges or incur costs related to settlements, legal fees, and corrective action plans. Additionally, public disclosure of investigation-related matters could harm our reputation and distract management from strategic initiatives.
label: Business Ethics & Values
reasoning: The paragraph fits Business Ethics & Values because it centers on whistleblower reporting mechanisms meant to detect “misconduct, including fraud, improper accounting, and violations of law or our code of conduct.” It explains that complaints may be unsubstantiated yet still trigger internal investigations, regulator inquiries, and significant costs, showing ethical and governance exposure from alleged misconduct. It also discusses potential retaliation allegations, noting anti-retaliation policies and the difficulty of proving absence of retaliatory motives. Corporate Governance could be a close alternative due to oversight and investigations, but the paragraph’s primary thrust is ethical misconduct reporting and handling, making Business Ethics & Values the correct label.
